title: Der Eisenhans
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 136. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly (Thüre, gieng, gerieth, todt).
about: KHM 136 is the tale that gave Robert Bly's men's-movement bestseller its title, though the Grimms' original is stranger and starker: a wild, rust-colored man is dragged up from a forest pool and caged, until the king's son frees him against orders and is himself driven out into the world. What follows is a long apprenticeship in disguise — a gardener's boy hiding golden hair under a cap, three secret battles won with borrowed help, and a slow recognition scene — before Iron Hans is revealed as an enchanted king restored by the prince's loyalty. It rewards a reader's patience with its middle stretch of repetition.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein König, der hatte einen großen Wald bei seinem Schloß, darin lief Wild aller Art herum.
sentences.l: There was once a king; he had a great forest beside his castle, and in it ran about game of every kind.
sentences.i: Once there was a king who had a great forest beside his castle, and game of every kind ran about in it.
sentences.n: “Es war einmal” is the fixed opening of a German tale — literally “it was once.” German needs no relative pronoun here: “der hatte” is a demonstrative doing the work of “who had.” “das Wild” is the collective noun for game, the deer and boar of a hunt — not the adjective wild, which is spelled the same and turns up in the next block. “herumlaufen” is separable (lief … herum).

sentences.t: Zu einer Zeit schickte er einen Jäger hinaus, der sollte ein Reh schießen, aber er kam nicht wieder.
sentences.l: At one time he sent a huntsman out, he was to shoot a roe deer, but he did not come again.
sentences.i: One day he sent out a huntsman to shoot a roe deer, but he never came back.
sentences.n: German runs the second clause on with a demonstrative — “der sollte,” and he was to — where English uses an infinitive of purpose. “sollte” is not moral duty but assignment: he was to. “nicht wieder kommen” is not to come back at all.

sentences.t: „Vielleicht ist ihm ein Unglück zugestoßen,“ sagte der König, und schickte den folgenden Tag zwei andere Jäger hinaus, die sollten ihn auf suchen, aber die blieben auch weg.
sentences.l: “Perhaps a misfortune has befallen him,” said the king, and sent the following day two other huntsmen out, they were to seek him out, but they too stayed away.
sentences.i: “Perhaps some misfortune has befallen him,” said the king, and the next day he sent out two other huntsmen to look for him, but they too failed to come back.
sentences.n: “zustoßen,” separable and with the dative, is what a misfortune does to a person: it befalls them. “den folgenden Tag” is a bare accusative of time, German’s way of saying “on the following day.” The 1857 text prints “auf suchen” as two words where modern German writes aufsuchen; “weg bleiben” is to stay away, not to return.

sentences.t: Da ließ er am dritten Tag alle seine Jäger kommen und sprach „streift durch den ganzen Wald und laßt nicht ab bis ihr sie alle drei gefunden habt.“
sentences.l: Then on the third day he had all his huntsmen come and spoke “range through the whole forest and do not leave off until you have found all three of them.”
sentences.i: So on the third day he had all his huntsmen summoned and said, “Range through the whole forest and do not give up until you have found all three of them.”
sentences.n: “lassen” with an infinitive is causative: “ließ … kommen,” had them come, summoned them. Note the small letter after the opening quotation mark — the 1857 edition begins direct speech without capitalising, and does so throughout this tale. “ablassen” is separable (laßt … ab), to leave off; “laßt” is the 1857 spelling of lasst.

sentences.t: Aber auch von diesen kam keiner wieder heim, und von der Meute Hunde, die sie mitgenommen hatten, ließ sich keiner wieder sehen.
sentences.l: But of these too came none home again, and of the pack of hounds that they had taken along, not one let itself be seen again.
sentences.i: But of these too not one came home again, and of the pack of hounds they had taken with them, not one was ever seen again.
sentences.n: “sich sehen lassen” — to let oneself be seen — is the ordinary way of saying that someone shows up or appears at all. “die Meute” is a pack of hunting hounds. German fronts the “von …” phrase and still keeps the verb second, which English cannot do; the literal follows it as far as it can bear.

sentences.t: Von der Zeit an wollte sich niemand mehr in den Wald wagen, und er lag da in tiefer Stille und Einsamkeit,
sentences.l: From that time on nobody would venture into the forest any more, and it lay there in deep stillness and solitude,
sentences.n: “von der Zeit an” is a framing pair (von … an, from … on) split around the noun. “sich wagen” is reflexive: to venture oneself somewhere — the verb wagen, to dare, not der Wagen, a wagon. “er” refers to der Wald, so English says “it”; and “die Stille” here is the noun, stillness, not the adjective still.

sentences.t: und man sah nur zuweilen einen Adler oder Habicht darüber hin fliegen.
sentences.l: and one saw only at times an eagle or hawk fly over it.
sentences.i: and only now and then was an eagle or a hawk seen flying over it.
sentences.n: “man” is the impersonal “one,” where English usually prefers a passive. “darüber hin” — over it and away — is the sort of doubled adverb German builds freely; hinfliegen is separable.

sentences.t: Das dauerte viele Jahre, da meldete sich ein fremder Jäger bei dem König, suchte eine Versorgung und erbot sich in den gefährlichen Wald zu gehen.
sentences.l: That lasted many years; then a strange huntsman presented himself to the king, sought a provision and offered himself to go into the dangerous forest.
sentences.i: That lasted many years; then a huntsman from elsewhere presented himself to the king, looking for a post, and offered to go into the dangerous forest.
sentences.n: “sich melden bei” is to report to someone, present oneself. “fremd” is strange in the old sense: from elsewhere, not known here. “eine Versorgung suchen” is to look for a living, a place that keeps you. “sich erbieten” is to offer of one’s own accord.

sentences.t: Der König aber wollte seine Einwilligung nicht geben und sprach „es ist nicht geheuer darin, ich fürchte es geht dir nicht besser als den andern, und du kommst nicht wieder heraus.“
sentences.l: The king, however, would not give his consent and spoke “it is not canny in there, I fear it will go no better for you than for the others, and you will not come out again.”
sentences.i: But the king would not give his consent, and said, “There is something uncanny in there; I fear it will go no better with you than with the others, and you will not come out again.”
sentences.n: “nicht geheuer” is the set phrase for a place that is uncanny or haunted; the word geheuer scarcely survives except in this negative. “es geht dir besser” is impersonal with a dative of the person: literally “it goes to you better.” The king says “du” to the huntsman, as a lord does to a servant.

sentences.t: Der Jäger antwortete „Herr, ich wills auf meine Gefahr wagen: von Furcht weiß ich nichts.“
sentences.l: The huntsman answered “Lord, I will risk it at my own peril: of fear I know nothing.”
sentences.i: The huntsman answered, “Sir, I will risk it at my own peril; I know nothing of fear.”
sentences.n: “Herr” is the address to a lord or master — the king, not God — and a servant uses it as this huntsman does. “wills” is “will es,” the pronoun clipped onto the verb — the 1857 text does this constantly. “auf meine Gefahr” is at my own risk. “weiß” here is the verb wissen, to know (von etwas wissen, to know of something), not the adjective weiß, white, which is spelled the same.

sentences.t: Der Jäger begab sich also mit seinem Hund in den Wald.
sentences.l: The huntsman betook himself then with his dog into the forest.
sentences.i: So the huntsman made his way into the forest with his dog.
sentences.n: “sich begeben” is the elevated verb for going somewhere — to betake oneself. “also” here means “so, thus,” not modern “also.”

sentences.t: Es dauerte nicht lange, so gerieth der Hund einem Wild auf die Fährte und wollte hinter ihm her:
sentences.l: It did not last long, then the dog got onto the trail of a head of game and wanted after it:
sentences.i: It was not long before the dog struck the trail of a piece of game and made to go after it:
sentences.n: “es dauerte nicht lange, so …” is a fixed narrative turn: it was not long before. “gerieth” is the 1857 spelling of geriet (geraten, to get into something by chance). “die Fährte” is the track of a wild animal. “wollte hinter ihm her” has no verb of motion at all — the “her” carries it — so English must supply one. “Wild” is again the noun, a head of game.

sentences.t: kaum aber war er ein paar Schritte gelaufen, so stand er vor einem tiefen Pfuhl, konnte nicht weiter und ein nackter Arm streckte sich aus dem Wasser, packte ihn und zog ihn hinab.
sentences.l: but hardly had he run a couple of steps, then he stood before a deep pool, could go no further, and a naked arm stretched itself out of the water, seized him and drew him down.
sentences.i: but hardly had he run a few steps when he stood before a deep pool and could go no further; and a naked arm reached out of the water, seized him and drew him down.
sentences.n: “kaum … so” pairs like English “hardly … when.” “konnte nicht weiter” leaves the verb of motion out, as German regularly does after a modal: could [go] no further. “der Pfuhl” is a slough, a deep muddy pool. The arm is the first we see of the wild man.

sentences.t: Als der Jäger das sah, gieng er zurück und holte drei Männer, die mußten mit Eimern kommen und das Wasser ausschöpfen.
sentences.l: When the huntsman saw that, he went back and fetched three men, they had to come with buckets and scoop the water out.
sentences.i: When the huntsman saw that, he went back and fetched three men, who had to come with buckets and bail out the water.
sentences.n: “gieng” is the 1857 spelling of ging. “die mußten” is the demonstrative again doing relative duty — “and they had to.” “ausschöpfen” is separable: to scoop out, to bail dry.

sentences.t: Als sie auf den Grund sehen konnten, so lag da ein wilder Mann, der braun am Leib war, wie rostiges Eisen, und dem die Haare über das Gesicht bis zu den Knieen herab hiengen.
sentences.l: When they could see to the bottom, there lay a wild man, who was brown of body, like rusty iron, and to whom the hair hung down over his face to the knees.
sentences.i: When they could see the bottom, there lay a wild man, brown of body like rusty iron, with his hair hanging down over his face to his knees.
sentences.n: The wild man — “der wilde Mann” — is a figure of German folklore: the hairy, enchanted being of the forest, a man under a spell. He is not a savage and the phrase is not a judgment on him; the tale’s last speech says outright that he was “in einen wilden Mann verwünscht.” “dem die Haare … hiengen” is a relative in the dative, the German dative of possession: literally “to whom the hair hung,” that is, whose hair hung. “Knieen” and “hiengen” are the 1857 spellings of Knien and hingen.

sentences.t: Sie banden ihn mit Stricken und führten ihn fort, in das Schloß.
sentences.l: They bound him with ropes and led him away, into the castle.
sentences.i: They bound him with ropes and led him away to the castle.
sentences.n: “Stricken” here is the dative plural of der Strick, a rope — not the verb stricken, to knit, which is spelled the same. “fortführen” is separable (führten … fort).

sentences.t: Da war große Verwunderung über den wilden Mann,
sentences.l: There was great astonishment over the wild man,
sentences.i: There was great wonder at the wild man,
sentences.n: German says “Verwunderung über” — astonishment over something — where English says “at.”

sentences.t: der König aber ließ ihn in einen eisernen Käfig auf seinen Hof setzen und verbot bei Lebensstrafe die Thüre des Käfigs zu öffnen,
sentences.l: but the king had him set into an iron cage in his courtyard and forbade on pain of death to open the door of the cage,
sentences.i: but the king had him put into an iron cage in his courtyard, and forbade anyone on pain of death to open the door of the cage,
sentences.n: “ließ … setzen” is the causative: had him set. “verbot” is the verb verbieten, forbade — not the noun das Verbot, a prohibition, spelled the same. “bei Lebensstrafe” is on pain of death; “Thüre” is the 1857 spelling of Türe. The iron cage starts the iron running through the tale.

sentences.t: und die Königin mußte den Schlüssel selbst in Verwahrung nehmen.
sentences.l: and the queen had to take the key into safekeeping herself.
sentences.i: and the queen herself had to take the key into her keeping.
sentences.n: “in Verwahrung nehmen” is the set phrase for taking something into safekeeping. “selbst” after the noun means “herself, in person” — and it is what puts the key under her pillow, where the boy can reach it.

sentences.t: Von nun an konnte ein jeder wieder mit Sicherheit in den Wald gehen.
sentences.l: From now on everyone could go into the forest again in safety.
sentences.n: “von nun an” is another split pair (von … an), from now on. “ein jeder” is a fuller everyone than jeder standing alone.

sentences.t: Der König hatte einen Sohn von acht Jahren, der spielte einmal auf dem Hof, und bei dem Spiel fiel ihm sein goldener Ball in den Käfig.
sentences.l: The king had a son of eight years, he played one day in the courtyard, and at the play his golden ball fell into the cage.
sentences.i: The king had a son of eight years old, who was playing one day in the courtyard, and while he played his golden ball fell into the cage.
sentences.n: “acht” here is the number eight, not the noun die Acht (heed) that appears later in the tale. “fiel ihm sein Ball” carries the dative of possession — literally “fell to him his ball” — where English says simply “his ball fell.” The ball, the boy and the cage are the machinery of the whole opening.

sentences.t: Der Knabe lief hin und sprach „gib mir meinen Ball heraus.“
sentences.l: The boy ran over and spoke “give me my ball out.”
sentences.i: The boy ran over and said, “Give me back my ball.”
sentences.n: “hinlaufen” is separable, to run over there. “gib … heraus” is herausgeben, to hand out, with the particle waiting at the end. The boy uses the familiar du to the wild man throughout.

sentences.t: „Nicht eher,“ antwortete der Mann, „als bis du mir die Thüre aufgemacht hast.“
sentences.l: “Not sooner,” answered the man, “than until you have opened the door for me.”
sentences.i: “Not before you have opened the door for me,” answered the man.
sentences.n: “nicht eher … als bis” is a fixed frame: not until. “aufmachen” is separable (aufgemacht), to open up; “mir” is the dative of the person concerned — open it for me.

sentences.t: „Nein,“ sagte der Knabe, „das thue ich nicht, das hat der König verboten,“ und lief fort.
sentences.l: “No,” said the boy, “that I do not do, that the king has forbidden,” and ran away.
sentences.i: “No,” said the boy, “I will not do that; the king has forbidden it,” and ran off.
sentences.n: “thue” is the 1857 spelling of tue (thun = modern tun). Both clauses put “das” first for weight and keep the verb second, an order English cannot copy; the idiomatic line rights it.

sentences.t: Am andern Tag kam er wieder und forderte seinen Ball: der wilde Mann sagte „öffne meine Thüre,“ aber der Knabe wollte nicht.
sentences.l: On the other day he came again and demanded his ball: the wild man said “open my door,” but the boy would not.
sentences.i: The next day he came again and asked for his ball; the wild man said, “Open my door,” but the boy would not.
sentences.n: “am andern Tag” is the next day (ander = other, following). “wollte nicht” leaves the infinitive to be understood: he did not want [to]. “öffne” is the imperative singular of öffnen.

sentences.t: Am dritten Tag war der König auf die Jagd geritten, da kam der Knabe nochmals und sagte „wenn ich auch wollte, ich kann die Thüre nicht öffnen, ich habe den Schlüssel nicht.“
sentences.l: On the third day the king had ridden out to the hunt, then the boy came once more and said “even if I wanted to, I cannot open the door, I have not the key.”
sentences.i: On the third day the king had ridden out hunting, and the boy came once more and said, “Even if I wanted to, I cannot open the door — I have not got the key.”
sentences.n: “wenn … auch” is concessive: even if. Again the bare “wollte” with the infinitive understood. Three days and three approaches: the tale counts in threes at every turn.

sentences.t: Da sprach der wilde Mann „er liegt unter dem Kopfkissen deiner Mutter, da kannst du ihn holen.“
sentences.l: Then spoke the wild man “it lies under the pillow of your mother, there you can fetch it.”
sentences.i: Then the wild man said, “It lies under your mother’s pillow; you can fetch it there.”
sentences.n: “er” is the key (der Schlüssel is masculine), so English says “it”: German pronouns follow the gender of the noun, which trips readers constantly. “sprach” is the tales’ narrative verb for “said,” far commoner than sagte.

sentences.t: Der Knabe, der seinen Ball wieder haben wollte, schlug alles Bedenken in den Wind und brachte den Schlüssel herbei.
sentences.l: The boy, who wanted to have his ball again, struck all misgiving to the wind and brought the key over.
sentences.i: The boy, who wanted his ball back, threw all misgiving to the winds and brought the key.
sentences.n: “Bedenken in den Wind schlagen” is the idiom: to throw one’s scruples to the wind. “Bedenken” is a noun here — misgiving, scruple — made from the verb bedenken, to consider. “herbeibringen” is separable, to bring here.

sentences.t: Die Thüre gieng schwer auf, und der Knabe klemmte sich den Finger.
sentences.l: The door went open with difficulty, and the boy pinched his finger.
sentences.i: The door opened only with difficulty, and the boy caught his finger in it.
sentences.n: “aufgehen” is separable (gieng … auf), used of a door that opens. “klemmte sich den Finger” is the dative of possession once more: literally “pinched himself the finger.” This small hurt is what later puts the finger into the well.

sentences.t: Als sie offen war, trat der wilde Mann heraus, gab ihm den goldenen Ball und eilte hinweg.
sentences.l: When it was open, the wild man stepped out, gave him the golden ball and hurried away.
sentences.n: “sie” is the door (die Thüre is feminine), so English says “it.” “heraus” is out toward the speaker and “hinweg” away from him: German marks the two directions in nearly every adverb.

sentences.t: Dem Knaben war angst geworden, er schrie und rief ihm nach „ach, wilder Mann, geh nicht fort, sonst bekomme ich Schläge.“
sentences.l: To the boy fear had come, he cried and called after him “oh, wild man, do not go away, otherwise I get a beating.”
sentences.i: The boy had grown frightened; he cried out and called after him, “Oh, wild man, do not go away, or I shall be beaten.”
sentences.n: “jemandem ist angst” is impersonal with a dative: literally “to the boy it was afraid,” meaning the boy grew afraid. “nachrufen” is separable (rief … nach), to call after someone. “Schläge bekommen” — to get blows — is the ordinary phrase for being beaten.

sentences.t: Der wilde Mann kehrte um, hob ihn auf, setzte ihn auf seinen Nacken und gieng mit schnellen Schritten in den Wald hinein.
sentences.l: The wild man turned about, lifted him up, set him on his neck and went with quick steps into the forest.
sentences.i: The wild man turned back, picked him up, set him on his shoulders and went with quick strides into the forest.
sentences.n: Three separable verbs in a row — umkehren, aufheben, hineingehen — each with its particle at the end of the clause. “der Nacken” is the nape, the back of the neck, where a child is carried; it returns in the battle, where the youth sits “ihnen auf dem Nacken,” right at their heels.

sentences.t: Als der König heim kam, bemerkte er den leeren Käfig und fragte die Königin wie das zugegangen wäre.
sentences.l: When the king came home, he noticed the empty cage and asked the queen how that had come about.
sentences.n: “zugehen” is separable and impersonal: to come about, to happen. “wäre” is the subjunctive of a question repeated at second hand — German marks reported speech this way, where English simply says “how it had come about.”

sentences.t: Sie wußte nichts davon, suchte den Schlüssel, aber er war weg.
sentences.l: She knew nothing of it, looked for the key, but it was gone.
sentences.i: She knew nothing about it, and looked for the key, but it was gone.
sentences.n: “er” is once more the key. “weg sein” is to be gone, missing. “wußte” is the 1857 spelling of wusste.

sentences.t: Sie rief den Knaben, aber niemand antwortete.
sentences.l: She called the boy, but nobody answered.
sentences.n: “rufen” with a bare accusative is to call someone, to summon them.

sentences.t: Der König schickte Leute aus, die ihn auf dem Feld suchen sollten, aber sie fanden ihn nicht.
sentences.l: The king sent people out, they were to look for him in the field, but they did not find him.
sentences.i: The king sent people out to search the fields for him, but they did not find him.
sentences.n: “ausschicken” is separable (schickte … aus). “sollten” is assignment again, not duty: they were to. “das Feld” is the open country outside the castle.

sentences.t: Da konnte er leicht errathen was geschehen war, und es herrschte große Trauer an dem königlichen Hof.
sentences.l: Then he could easily guess what had happened, and there reigned great mourning at the royal court.
sentences.i: Then he could easily guess what had happened, and great mourning reigned at the royal court.
sentences.n: “errathen” is the 1857 spelling of erraten, to guess. “es herrschte” — there reigned — sets a state over a whole place; the “es” is only a placeholder and means nothing in itself.

sentences.t: Als der wilde Mann wieder in dem finstern Wald angelangt war, so setzte er den Knaben von den Schultern herab und sprach zu ihm „Vater und Mutter siehst du nicht wieder, aber ich will dich bei mir behalten, denn du hast mich befreit, und ich habe Mitleid mit dir.
sentences.l: When the wild man had arrived again in the dark forest, he set the boy down from his shoulders and spoke to him “father and mother you will not see again, but I will keep you with me, for you have freed me, and I have pity on you.
sentences.i: When the wild man had come back into the dark forest, he set the boy down from his shoulders and said to him, “You will not see your father and mother again, but I will keep you with me, for you have set me free, and I have pity on you.
sentences.n: The speech runs on through the next two units, so the closing quotation mark does not come until the end of it. “Vater und Mutter” stands first for weight with the verb second — German can front an object like this and English cannot. “herabsetzen” is separable. What he says is exactly true: the boy did free him, and that debt is still being paid in the last paragraph of the tale.

sentences.t: Wenn du alles thust, was ich dir sage, so sollst dus gut haben.
sentences.l: If you do everything that I say to you, then you shall have it good.
sentences.i: If you do everything I tell you, you shall be well off.
sentences.n: “es gut haben” is to be well off, to have a good life; “dus” is “du es.” “thust” is the 1857 spelling of tust. “sage” here is the verb sagen, I say — not die Sage, a legend, which is spelled the same.

sentences.t: Schätze und Gold habe ich genug und mehr als jemand in der Welt.“
sentences.l: Treasures and gold have I enough and more than anyone in the world.”
sentences.i: I have treasure and gold enough, and more than anyone in the world.”
sentences.n: The object comes first again while the verb holds second place: “Schätze und Gold habe ich.” This offer is what he finally makes good at the wedding.

sentences.t: Er machte dem Knaben ein Lager von Moos, auf dem er einschlief, und am andern Morgen führte ihn der Mann zu einem Brunnen und sprach „siehst du der Goldbrunnen ist hell und klar wie Krystall:
sentences.l: He made the boy a bed of moss, on which he fell asleep, and the next morning the man led him to a well and spoke “do you see, the gold-well is bright and clear as crystal:
sentences.i: He made the boy a bed of moss, and on it he fell asleep; and the next morning the man led him to a well and said, “You see, the golden well is bright and clear as crystal:
sentences.n: “das Lager” is a place to lie, a bed made on the ground. “siehst du” is not a question here but the speaker’s nudge — you see — and the 1857 text gives it no comma. “Krystall” is the 1857 spelling of Kristall. The well is the trial of this part of the tale: whatever touches it turns to gold.

sentences.t: du sollst dabei sitzen und acht haben daß nichts hinein fällt, sonst ist er verunehrt.
sentences.l: you are to sit beside it and take heed that nothing falls in, otherwise it is dishonoured.
sentences.i: you are to sit beside it and take care that nothing falls in, or it is defiled.
sentences.n: “acht haben,” with the noun die Acht (heed), is to pay attention, to take care — nothing to do with the number eight, spelled the same way. “verunehren” is to rob of honour, to defile: the well is spoken of as something holy.

sentences.t: Jeden Abend komme ich und sehe ob du mein Gebot befolgt hast.“
sentences.l: Every evening I come and see whether you have followed my commandment.”
sentences.i: Every evening I shall come and see whether you have kept my commandment.”
sentences.n: German uses the present for the future: “komme ich” = I shall come. “das Gebot” is a commandment, the word used of God’s commandments, which suits the well’s sanctity.

sentences.t: Der Knabe setzte sich an den Rand des Brunnens, sah wie manchmal ein goldner Fisch, manchmal eine goldne Schlange sich darin zeigte, und hatte acht daß nichts hinein fiel.
sentences.l: The boy set himself at the edge of the well, saw how sometimes a golden fish, sometimes a golden snake showed itself in it, and took heed that nothing fell in.
sentences.i: The boy sat down at the edge of the well and saw how sometimes a golden fish and sometimes a golden snake showed itself in it, and he took care that nothing fell in.
sentences.n: “sich setzen” is reflexive — literally “set himself” — where English says sat down. “goldner” and “goldne” are the shortened forms of goldener, goldene. “sich zeigen” is to show itself, to appear.

sentences.t: Als er so saß, schmerzte ihn einmal der Finger so heftig daß er ihn unwillkürlich in das Wasser steckte.
sentences.l: As he sat so, the finger pained him once so violently that he stuck it involuntarily into the water.
sentences.i: As he was sitting there, his finger once hurt him so violently that he put it into the water without meaning to.
sentences.n: German makes the finger the subject — “der Finger schmerzte ihn,” the finger pained him — where English says he had a pain in his finger. This is the finger he pinched in the cage door; the tale forgets nothing. “unwillkürlich” is involuntarily, without willing it.

sentences.t: Er zog ihn schnell wieder heraus, sah aber daß er ganz vergoldet war, und wie große Mühe er sich gab das Gold wieder abzuwischen, es war alles vergeblich.
sentences.l: He drew it quickly out again, but saw that it was quite gilded, and however great trouble he gave himself to wipe the gold off again, it was all in vain.
sentences.i: He quickly drew it out again, but saw that it was gilded all over; and however hard he tried to wipe the gold off, it was all in vain.
sentences.n: “sich Mühe geben” is to take trouble, to try hard, and “wie große Mühe er sich gab” is concessive: however much trouble he took. “abwischen” is separable, and in “abzuwischen” the zu is wedged in between particle and stem — the regular pattern for separable verbs.

sentences.t: Abends kam der Eisenhans zurück, sah den Knaben an und sprach „was ist mit dem Brunnen geschehen?“
sentences.l: In the evening Eisenhans came back, looked at the boy and spoke “what has happened with the well?”
sentences.i: In the evening Eisenhans came back, looked at the boy and said, “What has happened to the well?”
sentences.n: Here the wild man is given his name, and this reading keeps it as it stands, untranslated: Eisenhans is Iron-Hans, Hans of the iron — his rust-brown body and the iron cage stand behind it, and it is the word the boy must shout at the forest edge later on. “ansehen” is separable (sah … an), to look at. “Abends” is a bare adverb of time.

sentences.t: „Nichts, nichts“ antwortete er und hielt den Finger auf den Rücken, daß er ihn nicht sehen sollte.
sentences.l: “Nothing, nothing” answered he and held the finger behind his back, so that he should not see it.
sentences.i: “Nothing, nothing,” he answered, and held his finger behind his back so that the man should not see it.
sentences.n: “auf den Rücken halten” is to hold something behind one’s back. “daß” with “sollte” gives purpose: so that he should not. German leaves both “he”s to be sorted out by sense; the idiomatic line names the man.

sentences.t: Aber der Mann sagte „du hast den Finger in das Wasser getaucht: diesmal mags hingehen, aber hüte dich daß du nicht wieder etwas hinein fallen läßt.“
sentences.l: But the man said “you have dipped the finger into the water: this time it may pass, but beware that you do not let anything fall in again.”
sentences.i: But the man said, “You have dipped your finger into the water; this time it may pass, but take care that you do not let anything fall in again.”
sentences.n: “mags” is “mag es”; “es mag hingehen” is the set phrase for letting something go, overlooking it. “sich hüten” is to be on one’s guard. “fallen läßt” is fallen lassen, to let fall, to drop, with both verbs stacked at the end.

sentences.t: Am frühsten Morgen saß er schon bei dem Brunnen und bewachte ihn.
sentences.l: At earliest morning he already sat by the well and guarded it.
sentences.i: At earliest morning he was already sitting by the well and keeping watch over it.
sentences.n: “am frühsten Morgen” is the 1857 superlative (modern frühesten): at the very first light.

sentences.t: Der Finger that ihm wieder weh und er fuhr damit über seinen Kopf, da fiel unglücklicher Weise ein Haar herab in den Brunnen.
sentences.l: The finger did him hurt again and he ran with it over his head, then unluckily a hair fell down into the well.
sentences.i: His finger hurt him again and he ran it over his head, and unluckily a hair fell down into the well.
sentences.n: “weh thun,” with the dative of the person, is how German says something hurts: “der Finger that ihm weh,” the finger hurt him. “fahren” with über is to run one’s hand over something. “unglücklicher Weise” is printed as two words in 1857 where modern German writes unglücklicherweise.

sentences.t: Er nahm es schnell heraus, aber es war schon ganz vergoldet.
sentences.l: He took it quickly out, but it was already quite gilded.
sentences.i: He quickly took it out, but it was already gilded all over.
sentences.n: “es” is the hair (das Haar is neuter). “herausnehmen” is separable.

sentences.t: Der Eisenhans kam und wußte schon was geschehen war.
sentences.l: Eisenhans came and already knew what had happened.
sentences.n: That he knows without being told is part of what he is; the tale states it flatly and never explains it.

sentences.t: „Du hast ein Haar in den Brunnen fallen lassen,“ sagte er, „ich will dirs noch einmal nachsehen, aber wenns zum drittenmal geschieht, so ist der Brunnen entehrt, und du kannst nicht länger bei mir bleiben.“
sentences.l: “You have let a hair fall into the well,” said he, “I will overlook it for you once more, but if it happens for the third time, then the well is dishonoured, and you can stay with me no longer.”
sentences.i: “You have let a hair fall into the well,” he said. “I will overlook it for you once more; but if it happens a third time, the well is defiled, and you can stay with me no longer.”
sentences.n: “nachsehen,” with a dative of the person, is to let someone off, to overlook a fault. “dirs” = dir es and “wenns” = wenn es, the clipped pronouns again. “entehrt” picks up “verunehrt” from the first warning: the same idea in two words.

sentences.t: Am dritten Tag saß der Knabe am Brunnen, und bewegte den Finger nicht, wenn er ihm noch so weh that.
sentences.l: On the third day the boy sat at the well and did not move the finger, however much it hurt him.
sentences.i: On the third day the boy sat at the well and did not move his finger, however much it hurt him.
sentences.n: “wenn … noch so” is the concessive frame: however much, no matter how. The third day is the one that undoes him — the pattern was fixed the moment three days were named.

sentences.t: Aber die Zeit ward ihm lang, und er betrachtete sein Angesicht, das auf dem Wasserspiegel stand.
sentences.l: But the time grew long for him, and he looked at his face, which stood on the water-mirror.
sentences.i: But time grew long for him, and he looked at his face as it stood on the surface of the water.
sentences.n: “die Zeit wird einem lang” is German for being bored: time grows long to you. “ward” is the old form of wurde. “der Wasserspiegel” — water-mirror — is the surface of the water, and the compound says exactly what happens next.

sentences.t: Und als er sich dabei immer mehr beugte, und sich recht in die Augen sehen wollte, so fielen ihm seine langen Haare von den Schultern herab in das Wasser.
sentences.l: And as he bent himself ever further over it, and wanted to look himself right in the eyes, his long hair fell from his shoulders down into the water.
sentences.i: And as he leaned further and further over, wanting to look himself right in the eyes, his long hair fell from his shoulders down into the water.
sentences.n: “sich beugen” is to bend oneself, to lean. “sich recht in die Augen sehen” — to look oneself properly in the eyes — is the boy admiring himself, which is why what follows fits him. “fielen ihm seine Haare” has the dative of the person again: whose hair it was and whom it happened to.

sentences.t: Er richtete sich schnell in die Höhe, aber das ganze Haupthaar war schon vergoldet und glänzte wie eine Sonne.
sentences.l: He straightened himself quickly up, but the whole head-hair was already gilded and shone like a sun.
sentences.i: He quickly straightened up, but the whole head of hair was already gilded, and shone like a sun.
sentences.n: “sich in die Höhe richten” is to straighten up. “das Haupthaar” is the hair of the head (das Haupt, head, in the elevated register). From here on the golden hair is the plot: everything turns on hiding it.

sentences.t: Ihr könnt denken wie der arme Knabe erschrack.
sentences.l: You can think how the poor boy took fright.
sentences.i: You can imagine how frightened the poor boy was.
sentences.n: The teller turns to his listeners and says “ihr,” you all — the one moment in the tale when he speaks to them directly. “erschrack” is the 1857 spelling of erschrak.

sentences.t: Er nahm sein Taschentuch und band es um den Kopf, damit es der Mann nicht sehen sollte.
sentences.l: He took his handkerchief and bound it around his head, so that the man should not see it.
sentences.i: He took his handkerchief and tied it round his head so that the man should not see it.
sentences.n: “band” here is the past of binden, to bind — not the noun das Band, a ribbon, which is spelled the same. This cloth is the first of the coverings; the little cap does the same work for the rest of the tale.

sentences.t: Als er kam, wußte er schon alles und sprach „binde das Tuch auf.“
sentences.l: When he came, he already knew everything and spoke “untie the cloth.”
sentences.i: When he came he already knew everything, and said, “Untie the cloth.”
sentences.n: “aufbinden” is separable — binde … auf — and means to untie: the particle auf here undoes rather than opens.

sentences.t: Da quollen die goldenen Haare hervor und der Knabe mochte sich entschuldigen, wie er wollte, es half ihm nichts.
sentences.l: Then the golden hair welled forth and the boy might excuse himself as he would, it helped him nothing.
sentences.i: Then the golden hair came welling out, and excuse himself as he might, it did him no good.
sentences.n: “quellen” is properly used of water welling up from a spring; of hair it makes it pour out. “mochte … wie er wollte” is the old concessive pattern, try as he might. “es half ihm nichts” — it helped him nothing — is the set phrase for “it was no use.”

sentences.t: „Du hast die Probe nicht bestanden und kannst nicht länger hier bleiben.
sentences.l: “You have not passed the test and cannot stay here any longer.
sentences.n: “die Probe bestehen” is to pass the test — the trial the tales set their heroes, and this is the one place where the hero fails it. The speech runs on through the next three units.

sentences.t: Geh hinaus in die Welt, da wirst du erfahren, wie die Armuth thut.
sentences.l: Go out into the world, there you will find out how poverty does.
sentences.i: Go out into the world; there you will learn what poverty is like.
sentences.n: “wie die Armuth thut” — literally “how poverty does” — is an old turn for what a thing feels like, how it treats you. “Armuth” is the 1857 spelling of Armut. “erfahren” is to learn by living through something, not by being told.

sentences.t: Aber weil du kein böses Herz hast und ichs gut mit dir meine, so will ich dir eins erlauben:
sentences.l: But because you have no wicked heart and I mean well by you, I will allow you one thing:
sentences.i: But because you have no wicked heart, and I mean well by you, I will grant you one thing:
sentences.n: “es gut mit jemandem meinen” is to mean well by someone; “ichs” = ich es. “eins” is “one thing,” neuter. He punishes and provides in the same breath — the tale never makes him an enemy.

sentences.t: wenn du in Noth geräthst, so geh zu dem Wald und rufe „Eisenhans,“ dann will ich kommen und dir helfen.
sentences.l: if you fall into need, then go to the forest and call “Eisenhans,” then I will come and help you.
sentences.i: if you fall into need, go to the forest and call “Eisenhans,” and I will come and help you.
sentences.n: “in Noth gerathen” is to fall into distress; “geräthst” is the 1857 spelling of gerätst. The name shouted aloud is the summons, and it is the promise the rest of the tale spends. Note that the German prints the name inside the speech with its own quotation marks; the apparatus uses English curly quotes for it.

sentences.t: Meine Macht ist groß, größer als du denkst, und Gold und Silber habe ich im Überfluß.“
sentences.l: My power is great, greater than you think, and gold and silver have I in abundance.”
sentences.i: My power is great, greater than you think, and I have gold and silver in abundance.”
sentences.n: “die Macht” is the noun power — not a form of machen, which is spelled the same. The object-first order returns in the last clause: “Gold und Silber habe ich.”

sentences.t: Da verließ der Königssohn den Wald und gieng über gebahnte und ungebahnte Wege immer zu, bis er zuletzt in eine große Stadt kam.
sentences.l: Then the king’s-son left the forest and went over made and unmade ways straight on, until at last he came into a great city.
sentences.i: So the king’s son left the forest and went straight on over roads made and unmade, until at last he came to a great city.
sentences.n: The tale calls him “der Königssohn” here for the first time since he was carried off — a reminder, just as he becomes a servant, of who he really is. “gebahnt” comes from die Bahn, a made track: beaten roads and pathless ground. “immer zu” is straight on, without stopping.

sentences.t: Er suchte da Arbeit, aber er konnte keine finden und hatte auch nichts erlernt, womit er sich hätte forthelfen können.
sentences.l: He sought work there, but he could find none and had also learnt nothing with which he could have helped himself along.
sentences.i: He looked for work there, but could find none, and he had learnt no trade with which he might have made his way.
sentences.n: “erlernen” is to learn a trade properly, not merely to hear about something. “sich forthelfen” is to help oneself along, to get by. “womit” is the compound relative German builds from wo- plus a preposition: with which.

sentences.t: Endlich gieng er in das Schloß und fragte ob sie ihn behalten wollten.
sentences.l: At last he went into the castle and asked whether they would keep him.
sentences.i: At last he went to the castle and asked whether they would take him on.
sentences.n: “ob” sends its verb to the end of the clause. “behalten” is to keep someone on, in service.

sentences.t: Die Hofleute wußten nicht wozu sie ihn brauchen sollten, aber sie hatten Wohlgefallen an ihm und hießen ihn bleiben.
sentences.l: The court-people did not know for what they should use him, but they had a liking for him and bade him stay.
sentences.i: The people of the court did not know what use to make of him, but they took a liking to him and bade him stay.
sentences.n: “wozu” is “for what, to what end.” “Wohlgefallen an jemandem haben” is to take a liking to someone — a noun where English uses a verb. “heißen” with a bare infinitive is to bid someone do something: “hießen ihn bleiben,” bade him stay.

sentences.t: Zuletzt nahm ihn der Koch in Dienst und sagte er könnte Holz und Wasser tragen und die Asche zusammen kehren.
sentences.l: At last the cook took him into service and said he could carry wood and water and sweep the ashes together.
sentences.i: In the end the cook took him into service and said he could carry wood and water and sweep up the ashes.
sentences.n: “der Koch” is the noun, the cook — though it is spelled exactly like the imperative of kochen, to cook. “in Dienst nehmen” is to take into service. “könnte” is the subjunctive of reported speech: the cook’s own words passed on. “zusammen kehren” is printed as two words in 1857 (zusammenkehren, to sweep together).

sentences.t: Einmal, als gerade kein anderer zur Hand war, hieß ihn der Koch die Speisen zur königlichen Tafel tragen,
sentences.l: Once, when just no one else was at hand, the cook bade him carry the dishes to the royal table,
sentences.i: Once, when no one else happened to be at hand, the cook bade him carry the dishes to the royal table,
sentences.n: “zur Hand sein” is to be at hand, available. “die Tafel” is the great board of a formal meal, not any table.

sentences.t: da er aber seine goldenen Haare nicht wollte sehen lassen, so behielt er sein Hütchen auf.
sentences.l: but since he did not want to let his golden hair be seen, he kept his little-cap on.
sentences.i: but since he did not want his golden hair to be seen, he kept his little cap on.
sentences.n: “sehen lassen” is to let be seen. “das Hütchen” is the diminutive of der Hut, a little cap — and from here to the recognition scene the cap and the hair beneath it are the whole action. “aufbehalten” is separable (behielt … auf), to keep on.

sentences.t: Dem König war so etwas noch nicht vorgekommen, und er sprach „wenn du zur königlichen Tafel kommst, mußt du deinen Hut abziehen.“
sentences.l: To the king such a thing had not yet come, and he spoke “when you come to the royal table, you must take off your hat.”
sentences.i: The king had never met with such a thing, and said, “When you come to the royal table you must take off your hat.”
sentences.n: “vorkommen” with a dative is for something to come one’s way, to be met with. “abziehen” is separable: to pull off. Bare-headedness before the king is a rule, not a courtesy, which is what makes the refusal so grave.

sentences.t: „Ach Herr,“ antwortete er, „ich kann nicht, ich habe einen bösen Grind auf dem Kopf.“
sentences.l: “Oh lord,” answered he, “I cannot, I have a bad scurf on my head.”
sentences.i: “Ah, my lord,” he answered, “I cannot; I have a bad scurf on my head.”
sentences.n: “der Grind” is scurf — a crusted sore on the scalp, a common and shameful complaint, and so the perfect excuse for keeping a cap on. It has nothing to do with modern grinsen, to grin.

sentences.t: Da ließ der König den Koch herbei rufen, schalt ihn und fragte wie er einen solchen Jungen hätte in seinen Dienst nehmen können; er sollte ihn gleich fortjagen.
sentences.l: Then the king had the cook called over, scolded him and asked how he could have taken such a boy into his service; he was to chase him away at once.
sentences.i: Then the king had the cook called in, scolded him and asked how he could have taken such a boy into his service; he was to drive him off at once.
sentences.n: “herbei rufen” is printed as two words in 1857 (herbeirufen, to call over). “hätte … nehmen können” is the subjunctive of a reported question. “der Junge” is the noun boy, lad — spelled like the inflected adjective jung, and used of the hero from here to the end of the tale.

sentences.t: Der Koch aber hatte Mitleiden mit ihm und vertauschte ihn mit dem Gärtnerjungen.
sentences.l: But the cook had pity with him and exchanged him with the gardener’s-boy.
sentences.i: But the cook had pity on him, and exchanged him for the gardener’s boy.
sentences.n: “Mitleiden mit jemandem haben” is the older form of Mitleid: to have compassion on someone. The exchange moves him from kitchen to garden — the two services the tale needs him in.

sentences.t: Nun mußte der Junge im Garten pflanzen und begießen, hacken und graben, und Wind und böses Wetter über sich ergehen lassen.
sentences.l: Now the boy had to plant and water in the garden, hoe and dig, and let wind and bad weather pass over him.
sentences.i: Now the boy had to plant and water in the garden, to hoe and dig, and to endure wind and foul weather.
sentences.n: Four bare infinitives in a row give the work its rhythm. “hacken” and “graben” are the verbs to hoe and to dig — not die Hacke, a mattock, or der Graben, a ditch, which are spelled the same. “etwas über sich ergehen lassen” is the set phrase for putting up with whatever comes.

sentences.t: Einmal im Sommer als er allein im Garten arbeitete, war der Tag so heiß daß er sein Hütchen abnahm und die Luft ihn kühlen sollte.
sentences.l: Once in summer when he worked alone in the garden, the day was so hot that he took his little-cap off and the air was to cool him.
sentences.i: Once in summer, when he was working alone in the garden, the day was so hot that he took off his little cap and let the air cool him.
sentences.n: “abnehmen” is separable (nahm … ab), to take off. “sollte” here is purpose rather than duty: so that the air might cool him.

sentences.t: Wie die Sonne auf das Haar schien, glitzte und blitzte es daß die Strahlen in das Schlafzimmer der Königstochter fielen und sie aufsprang um zu sehen was das wäre.
sentences.l: As the sun shone on the hair, it glittered and flashed so that the rays fell into the bedchamber of the king’s-daughter and she sprang up to see what that was.
sentences.i: As the sun shone on the hair it glittered and flashed, so that the rays fell into the king’s daughter’s bedchamber, and she sprang up to see what it was.
sentences.n: “wie” here means “as, when,” not “how” — you will meet this everywhere in the tales. “glitzte und blitzte” is a rhyming pair of verbs, and the literal keeps both. “um zu sehen” is the infinitive of purpose; “wäre” is the subjunctive of the reported question.

sentences.t: Da erblickte sie den Jungen und rief ihn an „Junge, bring mir einen Blumenstrauß.“
sentences.l: Then she caught sight of the boy and called out to him “boy, bring me a bunch of flowers.”
sentences.n: “anrufen” is separable (rief … an), to call out to someone. She addresses him simply as “Junge,” the ordinary word to a servant lad.

sentences.t: Er setzte in aller Eile sein Hütchen auf, brach wilde Feldblumen ab und band sie zusammen.
sentences.l: He set his little-cap on in all haste, broke wild field-flowers off and bound them together.
sentences.i: In all haste he put his little cap on, picked wild field flowers and tied them together.
sentences.n: Three separable verbs again — aufsetzen, abbrechen, zusammenbinden. “in aller Eile” is in all haste. Feldblumen are the flowers of the open field, as against the garden’s cultivated ones.

sentences.t: Als er damit die Treppe hinauf stieg, begegnete ihm der Gärtner und sprach „wie kannst du der Königstochter einen Strauß von schlechten Blumen bringen?
sentences.l: As he climbed the stairs with them, the gardener met him and spoke “how can you bring the king’s-daughter a bouquet of poor flowers?
sentences.i: As he was climbing the stairs with them, the gardener met him and said, “How can you bring the king’s daughter a bouquet of such common flowers?
sentences.n: “begegnen” takes the dative: “begegnete ihm,” met him. “schlecht” is bad in the sense of poor, common, of no quality. The speech runs on into the next unit.

sentences.t: geschwind hole andere, und suche die schönsten und seltensten aus.“
sentences.l: quickly fetch others, and pick out the finest and rarest.”
sentences.i: quick, fetch others, and pick out the finest and the rarest.”
sentences.n: “geschwind” is an old-fashioned quick, swift. “aussuchen” is separable (suche … aus), to pick out.

sentences.t: „Ach nein,“ antwortete der Junge, „die wilden riechen kräftiger und werden ihr besser gefallen.“
sentences.l: “Oh no,” answered the boy, “the wild ones smell stronger and will please her better.”
sentences.i: “Oh no,” answered the boy, “the wild ones have a stronger scent and will please her better.”
sentences.n: “die wilden” is an adjective standing alone as a noun — the wild ones — which German does freely. “gefallen” takes the dative of the person pleased: “sie werden ihr gefallen,” she will like them.

sentences.t: Als er in ihr Zimmer kam, sprach die Königstochter „nimm dein Hütchen ab, es ziemt sich nicht daß du ihn vor mir auf behältst.“
sentences.l: When he came into her room, the king’s-daughter spoke “take your little-cap off, it is not seemly that you keep it on before me.”
sentences.i: When he came into her room the king’s daughter said, “Take off your little cap; it is not fitting that you keep it on in my presence.”
sentences.n: “sich ziemen” is to be seemly, fitting — an old and formal verb. She says “ihn,” a masculine pronoun, although Hütchen is neuter: she is thinking of der Hut, the hat itself. The 1857 text lets the slip stand and so does this reading. “auf behältst” is aufbehalten, printed as two words.

sentences.t: Er antwortete wieder „ich darf nicht, ich habe einen grindigen Kopf.“
sentences.l: He answered again “I may not, I have a scurfy head.”
sentences.i: He answered again, “I am not allowed to; I have a scurfy head.”
sentences.n: “dürfen” is to be permitted — “ich darf nicht” is I am not allowed, a stranger answer than it looks: he makes the cap sound like a decency rather than a choice.

sentences.t: Sie griff aber nach dem Hütchen und zog es ab, da rollten seine goldenen Haare auf die Schultern herab, daß es prächtig anzusehen war.
sentences.l: But she reached for the little-cap and pulled it off, then his golden hair rolled down onto his shoulders, so that it was magnificent to look at.
sentences.i: But she reached for the little cap and pulled it off, and his golden hair rolled down over his shoulders, so that it was a splendid thing to see.
sentences.n: “greifen nach” is to reach for; “abziehen” is separable, to pull off. In “anzusehen” the zu is wedged into the separable verb ansehen — the regular pattern.

sentences.t: Er wollte fortspringen, aber sie hielt ihn am Arm und gab ihm eine Hand voll Dukaten.
sentences.l: He wanted to spring away, but she held him by the arm and gave him a hand full of ducats.
sentences.i: He tried to spring away, but she held him by the arm and gave him a handful of ducats.
sentences.n: “wollte” with an infinitive often means tried to, was about to. German says “am Arm” with the definite article where English uses a possessive. A ducat is a gold coin, and a handful of them is a small fortune to a garden boy.

sentences.t: Er gieng damit fort, achtete aber des Goldes nicht, sondern er brachte es dem Gärtner und sprach „ich schenke es deinen Kindern, die können damit spielen.“
sentences.l: He went away with it, but heeded not the gold, but rather brought it to the gardener and spoke “I give it to your children, they can play with it.”
sentences.i: He went off with it, but cared nothing for the gold; instead he brought it to the gardener and said, “I make a present of it to your children — they can play with it.”
sentences.n: “achten” with a genitive — “des Goldes nicht achten” — is the old construction for paying no heed to something; modern German would say “auf das Gold nicht achten.” “schenken” is to give as a gift. That he gives the gold away three times is how the tale shows what he is without ever saying it.

sentences.t: Den andern Tag rief ihm die Königstochter abermals zu er sollte ihr einen Strauß Feldblumen bringen,
sentences.l: The other day the king’s-daughter called to him once again he should bring her a bunch of field-flowers,
sentences.i: The next day the king’s daughter called to him once again that he should bring her a bunch of field flowers,
sentences.n: “zurufen” is separable (rief … zu) and takes the dative: to call to someone. German can open reported speech with no “daß” at all, as here — the clause simply follows.

sentences.t: und als er damit eintrat, grapste sie gleich nach seinem Hütchen und wollte es ihm wegnehmen, aber er hielt es mit beiden Händen fest.
sentences.l: and when he stepped in with it, she grabbed at once for his little-cap and wanted to take it away from him, but he held it fast with both hands.
sentences.i: and when he stepped in with them she snatched at once at his little cap and tried to take it from him, but he held it fast with both hands.
sentences.n: “grapsen” is a blunt everyday word for grabbing at something; the Grimms keep such words rather than smoothing them away. “wegnehmen” is separable, and “ihm” is the dative of the person it is taken from.

sentences.t: Sie gab ihm wieder eine Hand voll Dukaten, aber er wollte sie nicht behalten und gab sie dem Gärtner zum Spielwerk für seine Kinder.
sentences.l: She gave him again a hand full of ducats, but he would not keep them and gave them to the gardener as a plaything for his children.
sentences.i: She gave him another handful of ducats, but he would not keep them, and gave them to the gardener as playthings for his children.
sentences.n: “das Spielwerk” is an older word for a toy. The second refusal repeats the first almost word for word; the third, which follows, is told in a single line.

sentences.t: Den dritten Tag giengs nicht anders, sie konnte ihm sein Hütchen nicht weg nehmen, und er wollte ihr Gold nicht.
sentences.l: The third day it went no differently, she could not take his little-cap away from him, and he did not want her gold.
sentences.i: On the third day it went no differently: she could not get his little cap off him, and he would have none of her gold.
sentences.n: “giengs” is “gieng es,” it went. “er wollte ihr Gold nicht” has no infinitive at all — German lets “haben” be understood after wollen, and English must supply the sense. Three days again, and this time the third closes the episode instead of breaking the pattern.

sentences.t: Nicht lange danach ward das Land mit Krieg überzogen.
sentences.l: Not long after that the land was overrun with war.
sentences.n: “ward” is the old passive auxiliary, modern wurde. “ein Land mit Krieg überziehen” is the set phrase for making war on a country — to draw war over it like a covering.

sentences.t: Der König sammelte sein Volk und wußte nicht ob er dem Feind, der übermächtig war und ein großes Heer hatte, Widerstand leisten könnte.
sentences.l: The king gathered his people and did not know whether he could offer resistance to the enemy, who was over-mighty and had a great army.
sentences.i: The king gathered his men and did not know whether he could offer resistance to the enemy, who was overwhelmingly strong and had a great army.
sentences.n: “sein Volk” here is not the nation but the fighting men he can raise. “Widerstand leisten” takes the dative: to offer resistance to someone. Widerstand is the noun here, not a form of widerstehen.

sentences.t: Da sagte der Gärtnerjunge „ich bin herangewachsen und will mit in den Krieg ziehen, gebt mir nur ein Pferd.“
sentences.l: Then the gardener’s-boy said “I have grown up and want to go along into the war, only give me a horse.”
sentences.i: Then the gardener’s boy said, “I have grown up, and I want to go to the war with the rest — only give me a horse.”
sentences.n: “heranwachsen” is separable, to grow up. The bare “mit” means along with the others. He says “gebt,” the plural, to the men around him. Years have passed in a single sentence: the boy of eight is a youth.

sentences.t: Die andern lachten und sprachen „wenn wir fort sind, so suche dir eins: wir wollen dir eins im Stall zurück lassen.“
sentences.l: The others laughed and spoke “when we are gone, then look for one for yourself: we will leave one behind for you in the stable.”
sentences.i: The others laughed and said, “When we are gone, look for one yourself; we will leave one behind for you in the stable.”
sentences.n: “eins” stands for “ein Pferd,” which is neuter. “zurück lassen” is printed as two words in 1857 (zurücklassen, to leave behind). The mockery is the point, and what they leave him is the lame horse.

sentences.t: Als sie ausgezogen waren, gieng er in den Stall und zog das Pferd heraus; es war an einem Fuß lahm und hickelte hunkepuus, hunkepuus.
sentences.l: When they had marched out, he went into the stable and drew the horse out; it was lame in one foot and hobbled hunkepuus, hunkepuus.
sentences.i: When they had marched out he went into the stable and led the horse out; it was lame in one foot and hobbled along, hunkepuus, hunkepuus.
sentences.n: “ausziehen” is to march out to war. “hickeln” is a regional word for hopping or limping, and “hunkepuus” is the sound of the limp itself — a nonsense-word the Grimms print as it stands, and it sticks to the youth as a nickname later on.

sentences.t: Dennoch setzte er sich auf und ritt fort nach dem dunkeln Wald.
sentences.l: Nevertheless he mounted and rode away toward the dark forest.
sentences.n: “sich aufsetzen” — literally to set oneself up — is to mount a horse. “nach” with a place means toward, in the direction of.

sentences.t: Als er an den Rand desselben gekommen war, rief er dreimal Eisenhans so laut daß es durch die Bäume schallte.
sentences.l: When he had come to the edge of the same, he called Eisenhans three times so loud that it rang through the trees.
sentences.i: When he had come to its edge, he called Eisenhans three times, so loud that it rang through the trees.
sentences.n: “desselben” — of the same — is the stiff official way of saying “its,” and German uses it where English simply repeats a pronoun. The name is called three times, as such summons always are; the 1857 text prints it here without quotation marks.

sentences.t: Gleich darauf erschien der wilde Mann und sprach „was verlangst du?“
sentences.l: Immediately after, the wild man appeared and spoke “what do you demand?”
sentences.i: At once the wild man appeared and said, “What do you ask?”
sentences.n: “verlangen” is to demand, to ask for as one’s due. The question comes three times in the tale and always in these two words; this reading keeps it plain each time.

sentences.t: „Ich verlange ein starkes Roß, denn ich will in den Krieg ziehen.“
sentences.l: “I demand a strong steed, for I want to go into the war.”
sentences.i: “I ask for a strong steed, for I mean to go to the war.”
sentences.n: “das Roß” is a war-horse, a steed — set against “das Pferd” he already has. “denn” means “for, because,” and unlike weil it does not send the verb to the end.

sentences.t: „Das sollst du haben und noch mehr als du verlangst.“
sentences.l: “That you shall have, and more still than you demand.”
sentences.n: Object first and verb second again: “Das sollst du haben.” The promise of more than was asked is made good twice in the lines that follow.

sentences.t: Dann gieng der wilde Mann in den Wald zurück, und es dauerte nicht lange,
sentences.l: Then the wild man went back into the forest, and it did not last long,
sentences.i: Then the wild man went back into the forest, and it was not long,
sentences.n: “zurückgehen” is separable. The narrative turn “es dauerte nicht lange, so …” returns from the first block: it was not long before.

sentences.t: so kam ein Stallknecht aus dem Wald und führte ein Roß herbei, das schnaubte aus den Nüstern, und war kaum zu bändigen.
sentences.l: then a stable-groom came out of the forest and led a steed over, which snorted from its nostrils and was hardly to be tamed.
sentences.i: before a groom came out of the forest leading a steed that snorted from its nostrils and could hardly be held in.
sentences.n: “war kaum zu bändigen” is sein + zu, the German passive of possibility: hardly to be tamed, that is, could hardly be held. “der Stallknecht” is the man of the stable, a groom.

sentences.t: Und hinterher folgte eine große Schaar Kriegsvolk, ganz in Eisen gerüstet, und ihre Schwerter blitzten in der Sonne.
sentences.l: And behind followed a great troop of war-folk, wholly harnessed in iron, and their swords flashed in the sun.
sentences.i: And behind came a great troop of fighting men, armoured all in iron, and their swords flashed in the sun.
sentences.n: “das Kriegsvolk” is the fighting men taken together, the same Volk as above. “gerüstet” is armoured, harnessed, from die Rüstung, armour — which he is given himself at the festival. The iron of Eisenhans’ name is now a whole army.

sentences.t: Der Jüngling übergab dem Stallknecht sein dreibeiniges Pferd, bestieg das andere und ritt vor der Schaar her.
sentences.l: The youth handed over to the groom his three-legged horse, mounted the other and rode along in front of the troop.
sentences.i: The youth handed his three-legged horse over to the groom, mounted the other, and rode at the head of the troop.
sentences.n: “dreibeinig” — three-legged — is the tale’s joke about the lame horse; it is not literally short of a leg. “vor … her reiten” is to ride along in front.

sentences.t: Als er sich dem Schlachtfeld näherte, war schon ein großer Theil von des Königs Leuten gefallen und es fehlte nicht viel, so mußten die übrigen weichen.
sentences.l: When he approached the battlefield, a great part of the king’s people had already fallen, and it lacked not much, then the rest had to give way.
sentences.i: When he drew near the battlefield, a great part of the king’s men had already fallen, and it wanted little for the rest to be driven back.
sentences.n: “sich nähern” takes the dative. “gefallen” of soldiers means fallen in battle. “es fehlte nicht viel, so …” is the set phrase: it wanted little before. “weichen” here is the verb to give way, fall back — not the adjective weich, soft, spelled the same. “Theil” is the 1857 spelling of Teil.

sentences.t: Da jagte der Jüngling mit seiner eisernen Schaar heran, fuhr wie ein Wetter über die Feinde und schlug alles nieder was sich ihm widersetzte.
sentences.l: Then the youth came charging up with his iron troop, swept like a storm over the enemy and struck down everything that opposed him.
sentences.i: Then the youth came charging up with his iron troop, swept over the enemy like a storm, and struck down everything that stood against him.
sentences.n: “ein Wetter” here is not weather in general but a storm. “heranjagen” and “niederschlagen” are both separable. “sich widersetzen” takes the dative: to set oneself against someone.

sentences.t: Sie wollten fliehen, aber der Jüngling saß ihnen auf dem Nacken und ließ nicht ab bis kein Mann mehr übrig war.
sentences.l: They wanted to flee, but the youth sat on their necks and did not leave off until no man was left over.
sentences.i: They tried to flee, but the youth was right at their heels and did not leave off until not a man was left.
sentences.n: “jemandem auf dem Nacken sitzen” — to sit on someone’s neck — is the idiom for being right behind, at their heels; the same Nacken carried the boy into the forest. “ablassen” returns from the king’s first order at the opening of the tale. The tale does not soften the killing: not a man is left.

sentences.t: Statt aber zu dem König zurück zu kehren, führte er seine Schaar auf Umwegen wieder zu dem Wald und rief den Eisenhans heraus.
sentences.l: But instead of returning to the king, he led his troop by roundabout ways back to the forest and called Eisenhans out.
sentences.i: But instead of returning to the king, he led his troop back to the forest by roundabout ways, and called Eisenhans out.
sentences.n: “statt … zu kehren” is “instead of returning,” and the 1857 text prints zurück zu kehren as three words. “auf Umwegen” is by roundabout paths: he takes care not to be followed.

sentences.t: „Was verlangst du?“ fragte der wilde Mann.
sentences.l: “What do you demand?” asked the wild man.
sentences.i: “What do you ask?” asked the wild man.
sentences.n: The same two words as before — the tale keeps its formulas exactly, and expects the reader to hear the repetition.

sentences.t: „Nimm dein Roß und deine Schaar zurück und gib mir mein dreibeiniges Pferd wieder.“
sentences.l: “Take your steed and your troop back and give me my three-legged horse again.”
sentences.i: “Take back your steed and your troop, and give me my three-legged horse again.”
sentences.n: Two separable verbs in the imperative — zurücknehmen, wiedergeben — with their particles at the end. He asks for the lame horse back so that nobody will know him: the same instinct as the cap.

sentences.t: Es geschah alles, was er verlangte, und ritt auf seinem dreibeinigen Pferd heim.
sentences.l: Everything happened that he demanded, and [he] rode home on his three-legged horse.
sentences.i: Everything he asked for was done, and he rode home on his three-legged horse.
sentences.n: The second clause has no subject: German has just said “es geschah alles” and then carries straight on with the youth in mind, so the literal supplies [he] in square brackets.

sentences.t: Als der König wieder in sein Schloß kam, gieng ihm seine Tochter entgegen und wünschte ihm Glück zu seinem Sieg.
sentences.l: When the king came back into his castle, his daughter went toward him and wished him joy of his victory.
sentences.i: When the king came back to his castle his daughter went to meet him and wished him joy of his victory.
sentences.n: “entgegengehen” takes the dative: to go to meet someone. “jemandem Glück wünschen zu etwas” is to congratulate someone on something.

sentences.t: „Ich bin es nicht, der den Sieg davon getragen hat“ sprach er „sondern ein fremder Ritter, der mir mit seiner Schaar zu Hilfe kam.“
sentences.l: “It is not I who have carried off the victory,” spoke he, “but rather a strange knight, who came to my help with his troop.”
sentences.i: “It is not I who carried off the victory,” he said, “but a strange knight, who came to my aid with his troop.”
sentences.n: “den Sieg davontragen” is to carry off the victory. “sondern” is the “but” that follows a negative — not this but that. “fremd” again means unknown, from elsewhere.

sentences.t: Die Tochter wollte wissen wer der fremde Ritter wäre, aber der König wußte es nicht und sagte „er hat die Feinde verfolgt, und ich habe ihn nicht wieder gesehen.“
sentences.l: The daughter wanted to know who the strange knight was, but the king did not know it and said “he has pursued the enemy, and I have not seen him again.”
sentences.i: The daughter wanted to know who the strange knight was, but the king did not know, and said, “He pursued the enemy, and I have not seen him since.”
sentences.n: “wäre” marks the reported question once more. German keeps the perfect where English prefers a simple past: “er hat die Feinde verfolgt.”

sentences.t: Sie erkundigte sich bei dem Gärtner nach seinem Jungen:
sentences.l: She inquired of the gardener after his boy:
sentences.n: “sich bei jemandem nach etwas erkundigen” is to make inquiries of someone about something — a three-part frame the German builds around the two names.

sentences.t: der lachte aber und sprach „eben ist er auf seinem dreibeinigen Pferd heim gekommen, und die andern haben gespottet und gerufen "da kommt unser Hunkepuus wieder an."
sentences.l: but he laughed and spoke “just now he has come home on his three-legged horse, and the others have mocked and called ‘there comes our Hunkepuus again.’
sentences.i: but the gardener laughed and said, “He has just come home on his three-legged horse, and the others jeered and called out, ‘Here comes our Hunkepuus again.’
sentences.n: “eben” here is “just now.” The gardener’s speech runs to the end of the block, with the others’ mockery quoted inside it; the text as archived marks that inner quotation with a plain straight pair of marks rather than the German quotation marks of the outer speech, and it is reproduced here exactly as archived; the apparatus uses single curly quotes for it. “Hunkepuus” — the horse’s limp — has become the youth’s nickname. “ankommen” is separable (kommt … an).

sentences.t: Sie fragten auch "hinter welcher Hecke hast du derweil gelegen und geschlafen?"
sentences.l: They also asked ‘behind which hedge have you lain and slept in the meantime?’
sentences.i: They asked as well, ‘Behind which hedge have you been lying asleep all this while?’
sentences.n: “derweil” is meanwhile, all that time. The question is still inside the gardener’s speech, quoting what the others said.

sentences.t: Er sprach aber "ich habe das beste gethan, und ohne mich wäre es schlecht gegangen."
sentences.l: But he spoke ‘I have done the best, and without me it would have gone badly.’
sentences.i: But he said, ‘I did the best of all, and without me it would have gone badly.’
sentences.n: “gethan” is the 1857 spelling of getan. “es wäre schlecht gegangen” is the subjunctive of the unreal case: it would have gone badly. He tells the plain truth and is laughed at for it, which is exactly the joke the tale wants.

sentences.t: Da ward er noch mehr ausgelacht.“
sentences.l: Then he was laughed at still more.”
sentences.n: “ward … ausgelacht” is the old passive with ward (modern wurde). The closing quotation mark shuts the gardener’s long speech, which began several sentences back.

sentences.t: Der König sprach zu seiner Tochter „ich will ein großes Fest ansagen lassen, das drei Tage währen soll, und du sollst einen goldenen Apfel werfen:
sentences.l: The king spoke to his daughter “I will have a great festival announced, which is to last three days, and you shall throw a golden apple:
sentences.i: The king said to his daughter, “I will have a great festival proclaimed, to last three days, and you shall throw a golden apple:
sentences.n: “ansagen lassen” is the causative again: to have something announced. “währen” is an old verb for to last, endure. Throwing a golden apple is a way of choosing a husband: whoever catches it has claimed her.

sentences.t: vielleicht kommt der unbekannte herbei.“
sentences.l: perhaps the unknown one will come along.”
sentences.n: “der unbekannte” is an adjective used as a noun — the unknown one — and the 1857 text leaves it in small letters. German uses the present for the future once more.

sentences.t: Als das Fest verkündigt war, gieng der Jüngling hinaus zu dem Wald und rief den Eisenhans.
sentences.l: When the festival was proclaimed, the youth went out to the forest and called Eisenhans.
sentences.n: “verkündigen” is to proclaim publicly, a step above ansagen.

sentences.t: „Was verlangst du?“ fragte er.
sentences.l: “What do you demand?” asked he.
sentences.i: “What do you ask?” he asked.
sentences.n: The formula for the third time, now cut to the bone: the tale expects you to know by now who is speaking and how it will be answered.

sentences.t: „Daß ich den goldenen Apfel der Königstochter fange.“
sentences.l: “That I catch the golden apple of the king’s-daughter.”
sentences.i: “That I may catch the king’s daughter’s golden apple.”
sentences.n: The answer is a bare daß-clause with no main verb: it simply continues “I ask …”. “fange” is from fangen, to catch — the verb that governs each of the three days.

sentences.t: „Es ist so gut als hättest du ihn schon“ sagte Eisenhans, „du sollst auch eine rothe Rüstung dazu haben und auf einem stolzen Fuchs reiten.“
sentences.l: “It is as good as if you had it already” said Eisenhans, “you shall have a red armour to it as well and ride on a proud chestnut horse.”
sentences.i: “It is as good as though you had it already,” said Eisenhans; “you shall have a red suit of armour for it too, and ride a proud chestnut horse.”
sentences.n: “als hättest du” is the subjunctive of comparison — as if you had — with the verb thrown to the front. “ein Fuchs” of a horse is a chestnut, a horse of fox-red coat, not the animal: the three days give him a chestnut, a white and a black horse in turn.

sentences.t: Als der Tag kam, sprengte der Jüngling heran, stellte sich unter die Ritter und ward von niemand erkannt.
sentences.l: When the day came, the youth came galloping up, placed himself among the knights and was recognised by nobody.
sentences.i: When the day came the youth came galloping up, took his place among the knights, and was recognised by no one.
sentences.n: “sprengen” of a rider is to come at a gallop. “ward … erkannt” is the old passive: was recognised.

sentences.t: Die Königstochter trat hervor und warf den Rittern einen goldenen Apfel zu, aber keiner fieng ihn als er allein, aber sobald er ihn hatte, jagte er davon.
sentences.l: The king’s-daughter stepped forth and threw the knights a golden apple, but none caught it except he alone, and as soon as he had it, he galloped off.
sentences.i: The king’s daughter stepped forth and threw a golden apple to the knights, but no one caught it save he alone; and as soon as he had it, he galloped away.
sentences.n: “zuwerfen” is separable, to throw to someone, and takes the dative “den Rittern.” “als” after a negative means “except, save.” “fieng” is the 1857 spelling of fing.

sentences.t: Am zweiten Tag hatte ihn Eisenhans als weißen Ritter ausgerüstet und ihm einen Schimmel gegeben.
sentences.l: On the second day Eisenhans had equipped him as a white knight and given him a white horse.
sentences.i: On the second day Eisenhans had fitted him out as a white knight and given him a white horse.
sentences.n: “der Schimmel” is a white or grey horse. German names horses by their coats — Fuchs, Schimmel, Rappe — and needs no word for “horse” at all.

sentences.t: Abermals fieng er allein den Apfel, verweilte aber keinen Augenblick, sondern jagte damit fort.
sentences.l: Once again he alone caught the apple, but tarried not a moment, but rather galloped off with it.
sentences.i: Once again he alone caught the apple, but he did not linger a moment; he galloped away with it.
sentences.n: “verweilen” is to tarry, to linger — an elevated word. “sondern” is again the “but” that answers a negative.

sentences.t: Der König ward bös und sprach „das ist nicht erlaubt, er muß vor mir erscheinen und seinen Namen nennen.“
sentences.l: The king grew angry and spoke “that is not allowed, he must appear before me and name his name.”
sentences.i: The king grew angry and said, “That is not allowed; he must appear before me and give his name.”
sentences.n: “bös werden” is to grow angry; bös is the short form of böse. “seinen Namen nennen” is to name one’s name, to say who one is — the demand the whole tale has been evading.

sentences.t: Er gab den Befehl, wenn der Ritter, der den Apfel gefangen habe, sich wieder davon machte, so sollte man ihm nachsetzen und wenn er nicht gutwillig zurück kehrte, auf ihn hauen und stechen.
sentences.l: He gave the order, if the knight who had caught the apple made off again, then they should set after him, and if he did not return willingly, strike and thrust at him.
sentences.i: He gave the order that if the knight who had caught the apple made off again, they were to set after him; and if he did not come back of his own accord, to strike and thrust at him.
sentences.n: “sich davon machen” is to make off. “nachsetzen” is separable, to give chase. “habe” is the subjunctive of the reported order. This command is what wounds him on the third day — and the wound becomes the proof he offers.

sentences.t: Am dritten Tag erhielt er vom Eisenhans eine schwarze Rüstung und einen Rappen und fieng auch wieder den Apfel.
sentences.l: On the third day he received from Eisenhans a black armour and a black horse, and again caught the apple too.
sentences.i: On the third day he received a black suit of armour and a black horse from Eisenhans, and again he caught the apple.
sentences.n: “der Rappe” is a black horse, the third of the colour-names. Red, white, black on the three days: the tale dresses him afresh each time and lets the reader keep count.

sentences.t: Als er aber damit fortjagte, verfolgten ihn die Leute des Königs und einer kam ihm so nahe daß er mit der Spitze des Schwerts ihm das Bein verwundete.
sentences.l: But when he galloped off with it, the king’s people pursued him, and one came so near to him that he wounded him the leg with the point of his sword.
sentences.i: But when he galloped off with it, the king’s men pursued him, and one came so close that he wounded him in the leg with the point of his sword.
sentences.n: “ihm das Bein verwundete” is the dative of the person with the definite article — German says “wounded him the leg” where English says “wounded his leg”; the literal keeps the German shape to show it. “die Spitze” here is the point, the tip.

sentences.t: Er entkam ihnen jedoch, aber sein Pferd sprang so gewaltig daß der Helm ihm vom Kopf fiel, und sie konnten sehen daß er goldene Haare hatte.
sentences.l: He escaped them, however, but his horse sprang so mightily that the helmet fell from his head, and they could see that he had golden hair.
sentences.i: He escaped them nevertheless, but his horse sprang so violently that the helmet fell from his head, and they could see that he had golden hair.
sentences.n: “entkommen” takes the dative: to escape from someone. “der Helm ihm vom Kopf fiel” is the dative of possession once more. The cap has come off twice already; now the helmet does the same, and there is no hiding left.

sentences.t: Sie ritten zurück und meldeten dem König alles.
sentences.l: They rode back and reported everything to the king.
sentences.n: “melden” with a dative is to report to someone — the same verb the strange huntsman used of presenting himself at the start of the tale.

sentences.t: Am andern Tag fragte die Königstochter den Gärtner nach seinem Jungen.
sentences.l: The next day the king’s-daughter asked the gardener after his boy.
sentences.i: The next day the king’s daughter asked the gardener about his boy.
sentences.n: “fragen nach” is to ask after someone. “sein Junge” is his garden-lad, the boy in his charge.

sentences.t: „Er arbeitet im Garten: der wunderliche Kautz ist auch bei dem Fest gewesen und erst gestern Abend wieder gekommen;
